# **[Nigel Farage 's Justice Spokeswoman 'Covered in blood from head wound'
as police launch 'murder' manhunt](https://substack.com/redirect/1605c77a-5836-46fe-b072-520275cd3369?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
Former MP Ann Widdecombe was[ ](https://substack.com/redirect/8a6aa328-8749-4a34-80d3-768d2eff804a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**[found dead with a serious head wound](https://substack.com/redirect/8a6aa328-8749-4a34-80d3-768d2eff804a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** by her carer at her Dartmoor home in Devon triggering Devon and Cornwall Police to launch a **[murder investigation and manhunt for a white male suspect.](https://substack.com/redirect/e7e656fc-6e4b-458a-8ff5-af2babfb78e3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/1605c77a-5836-46fe-b072-520275cd3369?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **Carer Raises Alarm** : Panicked carer found the seventy eight year old covered in blood after sustaining a serious head injury at her Haytor property and alerted emergency services.
* **Murder Investigation Launched** : Officers called to the address around 11:40 am on Thursday confirmed the suspicious death with serious injuries and launched a full murder enquiry.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/1605c77a-5836-46fe-b072-520275cd3369?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **Suspect Search Underway** : Detectives believe the person responsible is a white male and appealed for CCTV doorbell or dashcam footage from the Haytor Vale area while increasing uniformed presence.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/1605c77a-5836-46fe-b072-520275cd3369?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **Tributes Pour In** : Reform UK leaders and politicians including Nigel Farage Richard Tice Keir Starmer and Shabana Mahmood paid tribute to Widdecombe's decades of public service and strong Christian values.

# [Meta breaches EU laws with addictive Instagram and Facebook designs](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The European Commission found Meta in breach of the Digital Services Act because Instagram and Facebook **[addictive design features like infinite scroll, autoplay push notifications](https://substack.com/redirect/a1c3fe44-ed19-4573-9f6b-99685b5d6fd0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** and personalized recommendations fail to address risks to physical well-being of minors and vulnerable adults.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **Addictive Features Cited** : Infinite scroll constantly shows fresh content while autoplay push notifications and highly personalized recommendation systems put users into autopilot mode.
* **Risks Ignored** : Meta ignored available information about young people spending time on platforms at night and how different content formats from reels to stories lead to excessive use.

# [America's most expensive states to live in 2026 exposed](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
CNBC's America's Top States for Business study identifies the **[10 most expensive](https://substack.com/redirect/f5419c26-c487-4dbd-be6b-a5053cd8352d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** and **[10 cheapest states](https://substack.com/redirect/f4154bbf-ea28-47ce-962c-29669ffbcd5d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** to live in 2026 where cost of living affects worker attraction and wage costs amid inflation at its highest rate in three years.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **Cost of Living Key** : CNBC rates states using the Council for Community and Economic Research index of prices for goods and services plus housing affordability for homeowners and renters and home insurance costs with the category worth 2% of each state's total score.
* **Expensive States Highlighted** : Illinois New York Washington and Connecticut received low cost of living scores of 17 out of 50 points earning D+ grades with high housing costs and rents punishing residents.
* **Cheapest States Bargains** : Missouri Ohio Kansas Iowa and Indiana earned higher cost of living scores of 34 to 36 out of 50 points with B+ or A- grades and lower rents around $1,565 to $1,582 dollars for three-bedroom homes.
* **Inflation Burden Varies** : Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh called inflation the most regressive tax harming the least well off with persistently high prices burdening Americans differently by state.

# [OCC grants Circle bank charter triggering 12% share surge](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Stablecoin issuer Circle received approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to operate as a trust bank **[allowing it to directly manage reserves for its USDC stablecoin](https://substack.com/redirect/81a6784e-4114-4ac2-9740-b9e2dc695629?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** with shares gaining more than 12% in early trading.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **Trust Bank Approval** : The new Circle National Trust eliminates need for third-party banks and custodians to hold cash and Treasury assets backing more than $73 billion dollars in USDC circulation.
* **Shares React Strongly** : Circle shares gained more than 12% in early trading following the announcement.
* **Regulatory Advantage** : The charter gives Circle a national bank regulator instead of varying state regulations that slow growth and increase costs.
* **Industry Trend** : The news reflects a broader trend where companies are trying to shift from financial applications to financial infrastructure.

# [Fed AI task force embraces AI's transformative economic revolution](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Federal Reserve Chairman[ ](https://substack.com/redirect/89c9b9c7-8afa-4f35-93fa-a4803272e88c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**[Kevin Warsh named AI task force members](https://substack.com/redirect/89c9b9c7-8afa-4f35-93fa-a4803272e88c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** including Marc Andreessen economist Charles I. Jones and Xbox CEO Asha Sharma all of whom share his bullish view on artificial intelligence boosting growth and productivity.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **Task Force Charge** : The group will assess economic impact of new general-purpose technologies including artificial intelligence to inform Federal Reserve policy judgments.
* **Members Optimistic Views** : Andreessen describes AI turning sand into thought Jones predicts possible growth exceeding 5% per year while Sharma affirms belief in AI.
* **Warsh Alignment** : The selections align with chairman view that AI adoption is major economic change potentially justifying interest rate cuts due to faster growth without inflation.
* **FOMC Skepticism** : Some FOMC participants noted uncertainty on timing and magnitude of productivity gains with concerns over AI demand shock raising electricity and semiconductor prices.

# [AI data center concerns shape Michigan Democratic Senate primary](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed highlights voter fears over AI and data centers as **[key issue in his tight Michigan Democratic Senate primary](https://substack.com/redirect/91dd162b-d3a6-4d1c-93b0-81b33b4d6054?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** against Rep. Haley Stevens ahead of the Aug. 4 vote with concerns coming up in every conversation.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **El-Sayed Guardrails Plan** : Candidate vows strict guardrails on data centers including job guarantees commitments to no utilities rate hikes and environmental protections.
* **AI Policy Unveiled** : El-Sayed proposed multi-pronged policy for AI including public ownership of the technology AI dividend mandatory divestiture from major tech companies and new tax on AI automation.
* **Stevens Approach** : Opponent as top Democrat on House Research and Technology Subcommittee focuses on expanded worker training human control of AI and ensuring no discrimination in employment education and housing.
* **Race Test Case** : Tight primary viewed as battle between progressives and moderates that could shape how Democratic candidates message on AI and data centers going forward.

# [Prediction markets spark insider trading fears at major firms](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Prediction markets have **[sparked insider trading concerns](https://substack.com/redirect/2eb62c7d-b4ab-4435-ad5d-5f8cab400ac7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** prompting companies including Goldman Sachs to ban employees from trading certain contracts related to bank-specific events elections financial markets macroeconomic data and geopolitics.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/b46d6741-9e0d-433a-a37b-3c4ddc7c8968?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **Goldman Sachs Ban** : The bank prohibits employees from trading on contracts related to events specific to the bank as well as elections financial markets macroeconomic data and geopolitics.
* **Google Employee Case** : CFTC and DOJ charged Google employee with using material nonpublic information to trade on Polymarket contracts related to browser Year in Search lists profiting $1.2 million dollars.
* **Company Responses** : Morgan Stanley has policies regarding trading on prediction markets in employee code of conduct while Bank of America is updating policies with examples of prohibited activities.
* **Compliance Challenges** : Lawyers note many firms are still early in addressing risks as platforms offer numerous contracts tied to company details.

All across North Carolina, folks keep telling me the same things - stuff just costs way too much. Families are getting hit hard by DC's reckless policies that are sending prices out of control on things like gas, utilities, groceries and housing.
I joined Dan Pfeiffer on Pod Save America to talk all about this race and the importance of flipping this seat to take back the U.S. Senate. We talked about how we need to roll back tariffs, restore health care cuts and critically think through policies that will help working class families.

America has a remarkably consistent way of responding when wealth becomes too concentrated and ordinary people begin demanding change.
It rarely confronts the concentration of wealth itself.
Instead, it redirects the pressure.
Think about it from the perspective of the elites. (Robber barons, billionaires, entrenched politicians and empire-managers):
First, bring in the workers the economy needs. Let them build railroads, harvest crops, staff factories, care for children and elders, fight your wars, and establish communities. Accumulate the riches to yourself.
Then, once wages stop keeping up with prices, housing becomes unattainable, and the general public starts asking why prosperity seems to flow only ever upward, point their anger sideways. Declare yesterday's workers today's invaders. Expand state power in the name of security. Fracture the coalition that might otherwise have demanded structural reform.
**America has repeated some version of this cycle for more than 150 years.**
The names change.
The targeted communities change.
The political slogans change.
The underlying mechanism? Barely does.
I want to show you the pattern. Because once you see it in the historical record, today's headlines stop looking like isolated events and start looking like another chapter in a very old American story.
And because this time, that story reached my own family.
Let's look at the structure, the history, the unprecedented advantages our generation has, and the levers for intervention we can pull.

### The First Model We Need to Understand
An article is making the rounds on Substack, answering the question most folks don't even want to ask aloud yet: "[How does this end?](https://substack.com/redirect/6929b622-7d0a-4a70-a202-384c96dc0eca?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)"
It's built on Peter Turchin's analysis of historical patterns of collapsing societies. Turns out, that can be mathematically modeled with strong predictive power: not prophesy, but systemic analysis with enough rigor to identify conditions that immediately precede structural disruption: revolution, civil war, collapse, conquest, reform, etc. Mapping when societies have accumulated socioeconomic conditions equivalent to an oversupply of deadwood in a forest... you can tell that the conditions are ripe for a wildfire, even if you can't exactly predict the spark.
His theory -- based on rigorous mathematical analysis of over 5,000 historical examples -- pivots on three major societal characteristics.
1. "**Popular Immiseration** ": This is what happens when wages and salary detach from growth, as we've all endured in America for the past 50 years; acutely for the past 30. The number of years your parents had to work to buy their first home, versus the number your kids will have to work to achieve the same milestone, is a precisely personal measure of "popular immiseration." The ~25% decline in actual American standard of living since my childhood in the 1990s, is a measure. Our record-levels of indebtedness, the suffocating student loans, the inability to afford healthcare or housing or even a $400 emergency expense for vast numbers of Americans... that's "popular immiseration," and it is the raw fuel for chaos or revolution.
2. The "**Wealth Pump** ": Economic and political structures that systematically transfer wealth from the middle and lower classes, to the upper echelon. Here we're talking about corporate monopolies, wage extraction, price gouging... every mechanism of billionaire profits at everyone else's expense - and, crucially, the political protection, complicity, endorsement, or outright facilitation of such extraction. This is the engine of both popular immiseration and the creation of an elite crust of society, who are disconnected financially and empathetically from the vast majority of their countryfolk. Think about the attitude of the health insurance and pharma CEOs vs. Americans who actually need healthcare. The billionaires vs. everyone else. As Occupy Wall Street so memorably put it, the 1% vs. the 99%. (Although it's closer to the 0.0001%.)

_Of note: America is currently suffering from levels of wealth inequality that rival the conditions that gave rise to the French Revolution. Marie Antoinette? Versailles? "Let them eat cake?" Yeah. No surprise to anyone reading this I'm sure, but... we're there._
3. "**Elite Overproduction** " and competition: Here is where it gets interesting. Revolutions throughout history -- including the American Revolution -- generally have not been led by the peasants or the poor folks themselves. The leaders are -- almost universally -- people who _should_ be of high status in their societies: upper-middle class upbringing, well educated, raised with the presumption that economic and/or political power were reasonable to expect from their future.
But when a society has too many of such people, and too few actual positions for them (...how many college graduates does America have? how many of us cannot find work?...), the resulting competition for scarce status leads some -- a critical few, the spark -- to build power _outside_ of the current structures. Historically speaking, disaffected potential elites harness the anger of the many to catalyze rebellion, structural reform, and/or revolutionary change.

Now, these three factors have all been at dangerously high levels in American society for some time now -- and worsening. Turchin accurately predicted in _Nature_ , back in 2010, that America would go through structural destabilization of some kind or another in the 2020s. Here we are.
Which is why his model's predictions for the range of possible outcomes are keenly relevant to today. Put simply:
* **Outright collapse** , including conquest by another nation
* **Lasting dictatorship** /authoritarian consolidation
* **Civil war** , of one kind or another
* _The good option:_ Broad-based **structural reforms** that relieve the economic pain of the majority enough to dissipate the pressure. *_(see below.)_

### The Layer That's Missing: Nativism as Release Valve
There's another very American cycle that's relevant to today, and it has to do with immigration. When labor is needed, immigrants are welcomed. As soon as they establish communities, put down roots, build businesses, begin to aggregate economic and political power... they are rebranded as invaders and/or threats, turned on, and unceremoniously evicted. (A very similar pattern pertains to Black Americans and other oppressed groups _within_ America, not just newcomers.)
Once you add that layer on top of Turchin's patterns, our current situation comes into much clearer focus. Here's what the data shows: when Turchin's three pressures build, the conflict they create is supposed to run _vertically_ -- ordinary people versus the small number of people capturing the gains. The 99% versus the 1%. That is how reform is won, or revolution is fought.
But that fight _almost never_ happens properly.
Instead, elites protect themselves -- and some aspiring elites cynically assist -- by redirecting the pressure _horizontally_ -- worker against worker, neighbor against neighbor. By turning an immigrant community into the scapegoat for a scarcity that **concentrated capital actually created**.
It follows the same six steps almost every time:
1. **Labor is invited.** The economy needs workers, so a community from another country is welcomed in -- railroads, agriculture, wartime production, care work, whatever the moment demands.
2. **The community establishes itself.** Over several generations, the community acquires property, builds businesses, earns credentials, gains social standing, sometimes achieves political power.
3. **The elite extraction limit hits.** Meanwhile, the wealth pump has been a-pumping. Housing and wages diverge. Popular immiseration hits. Credentialed people can't find the positions they were promised. The state starts to look incompetent. Anyone who has prosperity or stability -- _who doesn 't look like "us"_ -- starts to seem like a rival, or a threat.
4. **Scapegoating.** Rather than tackle structural reckoning with genuine social solidarity, some political faction weaponizes identity. It's entirely too easy to convince a poor white person to blame a poor Mexican person, rather than to blame the billionaire above them. (Particularly if, as now, that poor white person lives in one of the most propagandized societies on earth, and the elites pour money like gasoline into that fiery propaganda, to protect their own interests.)
5. **Oppression/Expulsion.** Exceptional state power gets normalized -- on noncitizens first. Authoritarianism is tested wherever it looks safest to do so. Raids, detention, deportation, disappearing due process... everything that protects the elite's power, is deployed. _While_ convincing enough of the majority group that "the government is protecting our interests!" to fracture genuine solidarity -- even though, _every time,_ the eviction of immigrant communities actually hurts **everyone** economically.
6. **Repression AND reform.** The authoritarian apparatus perfected on immigrants _migrates inward_. The same tools get turned on citizens, journalists, dissidents, and anyone who objects.
While silencing, neutralizing, or marginalizing the designated enemy, the capital-and-political elites _also_ turn their attention to appeasing the in-group. If enough people are protected, entertained, or buffered from the terrorizing of others -- or perversely gratified by it -- genuine solidarity can be sabotaged before it becomes effective enough to win real structural reform that would benefit **everyone** (except the elites).

With true solidarity neutralized, the elites win cover and retain power:
1. First, the immediate pressure of popular anger and immiseration in the in-group is relieved through turning against scapegoated immigrants, even against their own interests.
2. Then, the elites hand out _just_ enough structural reform to improve material conditions for the in-group who remains, relieving the pressure for awhile... while leaving untouched the underlying structural forces (elite power, extraction...) that produced it.

This isn't a one-time story. It's _the_ story, five times over.

### Five times, the same ending
Here's the history lesson. (Skip down if you want the likely trajectories from here, our unprecedented advantages, and what you can do to influence how this goes.)
Let's take a look at how the intersection of the immigrant "welcome-then-betray" pattern has played out against Turchin's three structural-compromise indicators, throughout the past 150 years of American history. It's eye-opening:
1. **Chinese Exclusion (1882).** In the 1850s and '60s, Chinese laborers were welcomed because America needed workers--for mines, agriculture, factories, and especially the railroads that made the fortunes of the emerging Gilded Age. Chinese workers built lives and communities alongside the infrastructure they built for the country. Then the depression of the 1870s hit. Wages fell, jobs became scarce, and the robber-baron economy generated immense fortunes above, and widespread insecurity below. Rather than force railroad magnates, financiers, and industrialists to surrender their growing power, political leaders and labor demagogues recast Chinese workers as "unassimilable" competitors responsible for white hardship. The result was mob violence, massacres, forced expulsions, discriminatory local laws, and finally the first major federal law excluding an entire nationality of laborers.

The bargain offered to white workers was racial protection _in place of_ economic power: restrict Chinese competition, preserve certain jobs for the in-group, and promise that exclusion would restore security. **But** the fortunes accumulated by railroad owners and financiers **were not redistributed**. Corporate power was not broken. White workers did not gain ownership of the economy they had helped build. Exclusion provided enough psychological status and limited labor-market protection to _fracture the coalition_ that might have confronted the robber barons directly. The deeper reckoning arrived later, through the Populist and Progressive movements: antitrust enforcement, railroad regulation, food and workplace protections, democratic reforms, and the beginnings of organized labor power. Those reforms restrained parts of the Gilded Age order--but they developed inside a political system that had already expelled Chinese workers from the coalition entitled to benefit.
2. **The Palmer Raids (1919 -20).** After World War One, millions of troops were demobilized into the labor market, wartime inflation devoured wages, and workers launched one of the largest strike waves in American history. The Russian Revolution, several genuine anarchist bombings, and elite fear of organized labor were fused into a single manufactured enemy: immigrant, radical, anarchist, socialist, union organizer, "national-security threat."

Under Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer and the young J. Edgar Hoover, federal agents raided homes and meeting halls, arrested thousands, and deported hundreds--often without warrants, reliable evidence, access to counsel, or meaningful due process. Immigrant radicals were the most vulnerable targets, but the broader purpose was to terrorize the labor movement and teach native-born workers that solidarity with "foreign agitators" would place them outside respectable American society. In exchange, the protected in-group was offered normalcy: patriotic belonging, relief from wartime upheaval, rising consumer abundance for those able to access it, and a government explicitly aligned with business. The 1920s weakened unions, concentrated wealth, cut taxes at the top, and elevated the businessman and millionaire as national heroes. **Repression had relieved the political pressure without repairing the economic structure.** Less than a decade later, in the great crash of 1929, the speculative, debt-driven order built on top of that inequality imploded anyway.
3. **Mexican Repatriation (1930s).** Mexican workers had been actively recruited for American agriculture, mining, railroads, and industry--particularly when World War One and earlier immigration restrictions produced labor shortages. Then the economy built by the Gilded Age's monopolists and the 1920s financial elite collapsed. The people whose work had been indispensable were suddenly blamed for unemployment, falling wages, and pressure on public relief. Local, state, and federal authorities pressured, deceived, rounded up, and transported hundreds of thousands of people across the border. Many were American citizens, including children born here, because the state was never carefully sorting by citizenship. It was sorting by ancestry, surname, neighborhood, and who looked like the designated enemy.

At the same time, the New Deal finally delivered a substantial portion of the structural reform Populists, Progressives, unionists, and socialists had demanded for decades: banking regulation, public employment, Social Security, collective-bargaining rights, infrastructure, and new limits on corporate power. Those reforms were real. They materially improved millions of lives, strengthened organized labor, built a mass middle class, and helped save American democracy.

But the political settlement was racially bounded. Agricultural and domestic workers were initially excluded from central protections, preserving the power of Southern landowners and other employers while leaving disproportionately Black and Mexican American workers outside much of the new social contract. Repression removed part of the working class; exclusion kept another part cheap and politically weak; reform gave enough security and bargaining power to the protected in-group to stabilize the country. The wealth pump was significantly constrained--but America avoided having to extend equal economic citizenship to everyone whose labor had built it.
4. **The Bracero Program and the 1954 deportation campaign.** During World War Two, the federal government again faced a labor shortage and created the Bracero Program, importing Mexican men on temporary contracts to work in agriculture and on the railroads. The program continued until 1964 and brought millions of workers into the United States--but on terms that tied their legal presence and economic survival closely to the employers who hired them. Then, in 1954, the government launched a highly publicized, racially named mass-deportation campaign against other Mexican workers and communities, even while growers continued to demand--and the federal government continued to import--Mexican labor.

The contradiction reveals the actual structure. The goal was never simply to remove Mexican workers. American agriculture still depended on them. The goal was to **separate labor from belonging:** to preserve access to the workforce while stripping that workforce of permanence, security, bargaining power, and the practical ability to say no. Employers received a controlled and replaceable labor supply. Native-born workers were told that the government was protecting their jobs and borders. Mexican American citizens were pressured to distinguish themselves from the newly criminalized "illegal" worker, weakening solidarity inside the community itself. Meanwhile, the protected majority received the broader benefits of the postwar settlement--union wages, subsidized mortgages, public infrastructure, expanding education, and the promise of middle-class security--although many of those benefits were distributed through racially discriminatory institutions. The United States could therefore sustain a generous social contract for much of its in-group while keeping a politically vulnerable population available to exploit while performing essential work beneath it.
5. **Japanese incarceration.** Japanese immigrants had also been welcomed where their labor was needed, particularly in western agriculture. Over time, Japanese American families built farms, businesses, schools, houses of worship, and civic institutions despite laws barring many first-generation immigrants from naturalization and restricting their ability to own land. After Pearl Harbor, wartime fear, racial hostility, economic envy, and claims of national security merged. More than 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry were forcibly removed from their homes and incarcerated; approximately two-thirds were United States citizens.

The government did not conduct individualized investigations to determine who had committed an offense. It designated an entire ancestry as presumptively foreign. Families lost homes, farms, businesses, and years of freedom, while neighboring landowners and commercial competitors sometimes acquired the property and economic space they left behind. The majority population was offered both reassurance and material advantage: the government appeared decisive, the internal "threat" appeared contained, and valuable assets and opportunities were transferred away from the targeted community.

At the same time, the wartime state delivered extraordinary benefits and social incorporation to much of the protected population--full employment, unionized industrial wages, military benefits, subsidized education, and eventually government-backed pathways into homeownership. Japanese American soldiers could prove their loyalty through exceptional sacrifice, but their families' citizenship had not protected them at home. Once "foreign" becomes a racial category rather than a legal one, _citizenship stops functioning as a shield._

**Every single time, the scapegoating succeeds politically while failing as a genuine economic remedy.** It may produce limited advantages for parts of the in-group: one category of job reserved, a competitor expelled, a government benefit extended, a union contract protected, a mortgage subsidized, a feeling of restored status or safety. _Those gains are not always imaginary._ That is precisely why the bargain works. But they are _carefully bounded_. They relieve enough pressure to undermine the broader solidarity that **could have won deeper change,** while leaving the commanding heights of wealth and political power largely intact.
And when structural reform finally comes, it comes divided. Antitrust and workplace reform alongside Chinese exclusion. Postwar prosperity alongside deportation and racialized "guest" labor. The New Deal for those its programs were built to include, with Black, Mexican American, agricultural, and domestic workers excluded from crucial protections. The GI Bill and federally supported homeownership administered through systems that blocked many families of color. Liberal democracy and due process for the presumed American in-group; surveillance, detention, expulsion, or dispossession for the population cast as foreign.
This is the pattern the Turchin article doesn't name: _America 's historical "exit" has rarely been a clean choice between reform and collapse_. More often, it has been **reform for some, paired with repression of others** --enough material protection for the in-group to stabilize the system, purchased through the exclusion, exploitation, or expulsion of the people whose solidarity might otherwise have made deeper transformation possible.
The brilliance--and the horror--of the arrangement is that the in-group _does_ receive something. Not enough to become free of elite domination. Not enough to end the wealth pump permanently. But enough to persuade many people that **defending their relative position is safer than joining with the designated "enemy" to demand a fundamentally different order.**

### Where we are right now
Let's catch up to the present moment and look at the numbers.
As of April 2026, ICE was holding more than 60,000 people -- over 70% percent with no criminal conviction at all, and the vast majority of the rest with misdemeanors. But point-in-time detention numbers are only the snapshot; _**removals**_ are the throughput, and that tells the real story. **ICE reported nearly 320,000 removals in FY2025, and early FY2026 data point toward a pace above 430,000 a year.** That's hundreds of thousands of hardworking, contributing community members, _gone_ , plus whoever of their family left to follow them. This is not a system narrowly targeting violent criminals. It's one of the largest coercive administrative systems in the federal government, running full-tilt against a politically vulnerable out-group.
Meanwhile, V-Dem recorded a historic 24% single-year collapse in the U.S. Liberal Democracy Index, dropping the country from 20th to 51st in the world. And underneath that increase in authoritarianism sits the wealth pump itself: the top 10% of households own more than two-thirds of household wealth, the top 1% alone owns almost as much as the bottom 90 percent combined, and the median home now costs roughly 5x median household income, up from about 3x a generation ago. That's not a prediction. That's the wealth pump, measured, in real time -- running at the exact moment the "foreigner" sorting mechanism is running too. Stages 4 and 5, with forays into 6, are live right now.
Inside corporate America, the extraction is even easier to see. Across the S&P 500, CEOs were paid about 285x their median worker in 2024, versus roughly 21x in 1965. **What does a nominal $2 wage increase mean to a normal worker, when the CEO used to be making 30x your pay and is now making 300x?**
Among the 100 major companies with the lowest median wages, the ratio hit 632 to one -- average CEO pay near $17.2 million against a median worker earning $35,570. At Starbucks, the reported ratio topped 6,600 to 1. It's tempting to say America is now more unequal than France on the eve of its revolution. Truthfully -- the records are incomplete, but the comparison is no longer absurd. We've built, inside a nominal democracy, a level of wealth concentration recognizable as aristocratic.

### The trajectories, briefly
Turchin's pattern gives you a range of outcomes:
* **Most likely (roughly even odds):** uneven authoritarian consolidation -- elections continue, but detention, surveillance, and selective enforcement quietly expand for whoever's been designated the internal enemy, while daily life stays normal enough for everyone else that the warnings sound exaggerated.
* **Second most likely:** an actual reform exit -- the Progressive Era/New Deal kind -- but _only if the coalition that wins it refuses to leave anyone out this time._
* **Less likely but not remote:** acute civil rupture -- not armies on a front line, necessarily, but other forms of civil war: disputed elections, federal-state standoffs, and political violence that rival elites may start but can't always control.

The patterns of American history give you a strong likelihood:
**Immigrants or racially-profiled minorities will be scapegoated, imprisoned, and expelled. So will anyone who supports them. Authoritarianism may consolidate, and billionaire power will almost certainly persist, but the in-group will be granted enough psychological status and material relief to get them to go along.**

## Why this time could - truly - be different
History repeats itself--but never under identical conditions.
There are reasons for hope that previous generations simply did not have.
For most of American history, the people being scapegoated were largely unable to tell their own stories. Chinese railroad workers could not livestream an expulsion. Japanese American families could not upload footage from incarceration camps. Mexican American citizens rounded up during the Depression could not instantly show the country what was happening to them. News flowed **downward** through a handful of newspapers, radio stations, and television networks. If powerful institutions decided on the narrative, most people never encountered an alternative.
That world is gone.
Today, millions of ordinary people carry cameras in our pockets. A raid in Tacoma can be seen in Miami an hour later. An ICE detention center in Washington can become the concern of a church in Georgia, a veterans' organization in Texas, or a labor union in Michigan. Propaganda still exists--at industrial scale--but so does the ability to document reality _before_ someone else has the chance to rewrite it.
Something else is different.
America is no longer isolated from the rest of the world. Most of us now have genuine friendships, family ties, professional relationships, and communities that cross national, racial, and religious lines. Millions of Americans have immigrant spouses. Children who speak more than one language. Coworkers from every continent. Veterans who fought beside interpreters they still consider family. Faith communities that are themselves multinational. It is much harder to convince people that "those people" are aliens when "those people" are your neighbors, your coworkers, your son-in-law, your mosque, your church, your child's teacher.
The elite playbook still functions. But it doesn't work as automatically as it once did.
Most importantly, **we understand the pattern** better than previous generations did. Peter Turchin's work gives us one lens. History gives us another. We can watch the pressure building. We can recognize the wealth pump. We can see the scapegoating while it is happening--not decades later in a history book.
That creates a possibility our predecessors could never reach.
The greatest advantage any manipulation has is that the target doesn't realize they're being manipulated.
**Once enough people recognize the mechanism, it begins to lose its power.**
The ending is not written.
The same American history that teaches us how democracies drift toward oligarchy and turn against the people who built them, also teaches us that ordinary people like you and me, acting together across the lines they were told to fear, have repeatedly forced this country to become more than its elites intended.
That possibility still exists.
But only if we refuse, this time, to let them convince us that our neighbors are the enemy when the real question has always been **who benefits from us fighting each other.**
* * *
### What you can actually do
Not just "be kinder" -- although building relationships with people you disagree with politically is worthwhile, albeit uncomfortable, and can be a **real firebreak** , when the spark comes. Here are structural approaches as well:
* **Build solidarity before the emergency** , not after -- unions, congregations, neighborhood networks, immigrant-veteran alliances. People defend who they understand as genuinely part of their own "we." _Build the "we."_
* **Defend due process and the rule of law** _**universally**_**.** The moment you accept a lower standard for someone unpopular, you've built the tool that will get used on your friends, your loved ones, and eventually you next.
* **Document everything, rigorously** -- names, badge numbers, dates, outcomes. Organize _everything_. Preserve multiple copies. Save it offline, in local storage and physical locations. Share it with trusted friends. Evidentiary architecture is what lets the truth survive contact with power. _Ask me how I know._
* **Make healthcare and housing a** _**democracy**_**issue** -- because a generation that can't form a household, access medical care, or believe in the future is a generation susceptible to manipulation, gaslighting, and temptation to join the enforcers (eg. ICE) out of sheer economic desperation.
* **Create honorable off-ramps for elite defectors** -- When people who hold power -- of any kind, financial, civil, political, social... -- decide that they don't want to uphold this regime anymore, _welcome them_. They are essential for actual victory. Demanding humiliation from new allies is a **strong disincentive** for them to come join us...and we need them. Reform happens when elite defection is possible and rewarded, not just when protest is loud.
* **Share the knowledge**. The more people can see through the pattern, the better chance we all have of successfully resisting the gaslighting, scapegoating, bribery, betrayal, and propaganda machine being used on us in real-time. We can break this pattern... but we have to do it _**together**_**.**

### This is personal
My husband, Zahid, is an honorable, patriotic, decorated, 100% disabled United States military veteran. He has lived in America for decades. He is disabled in wheelchair due to injuries sustained on active duty. He survived a broken back and traumatic brain injury, among other injuries, in service to this country. He has no U.S. criminal record. He is the father of our two young American children.
Last year, ICE illegally abducted him and locked him inside the Northwest ICE Processing Center for 124 days anyway.
That happened because the sorting mechanism I have described throughout this article is real. Once institutions begin sorting people primarily into categories instead of judging them as individuals under the law, the facts that ought to matter begin to disappear. Military service. Disability. Family. Character. Decades of contributing to our community. None of it protected him.
The machinery had decided which box he belonged in.
So we fought.
Not just in the court of public opinion. In federal court. In immigration court. At the BIA. In the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, one level below the Supreme Court.
Across four separate federal jurisdictions, with no attorney. We documented everything. We challenged everything. We refused to disappear quietly into the administrative machinery of state terror. And eventually, a federal judge ordered Zahid's immediate release, concluding that what had happened was, in the court's own words, "flat out wrong." (_Chaudhry v. Bondi_ , No. 2:25-cv-02339, W.D. Wash.)
I'm not telling you this because it's extraordinary.
**I 'm telling you because it isn't.**
It is exactly what this historical pattern predicts: extraordinary coercive power first deployed against the people least likely to be defended, justified by broad categories instead of individualized justice, and normalized one case at a time. The only reason you know Zahid's name, instead of one of the _**hundreds of thousands**_ of others who pass through that system, is that we refused to let his story disappear.
If you want someone in Congress who has not only studied these patterns in history, but has stood inside them--who has defended constitutional due process when it landed like a meteor in my life, who has confronted a weaponized federal government and prevailed, who knows from lived experience what abusive government power feels like when it is turned against an ordinary family--I'm asking for your vote, your voice, and whatever support you can give.
I'm Melissa Chaudhry: a Constitutional Democrat, community-rooted leader, published author, and proven fighter for liberty and justice. I don't answer to corporate PACs, foreign interests, or defense contractors. I answer to the Constitution of the United States of America -- and to We the People, _who only get real victory if we fight**together.**_

When wealth concentrates, wages stagnate, and normal folks begin asking the right questions, American politics runs the same play: scapegoat immigrants, fracture solidarity, and appease the in-group. | | | Jul 10 | | | | | | | | | | | | America has a remarkably consistent way of responding when wealth becomes too concentrated and ordinary people begin demanding change. It rarely confronts the concentration of wealth itself. Instead, it redirects the pressure. Think about it from the perspective of the elites. (Robber barons, billionaires, entrenched politicians and empire-managers): First, bring in the workers the economy needs. Let them build railroads, harvest crops, staff factories, care for children and elders, fight your wars, and establish communities. Accumulate the riches to yourself. Then, once wages stop keeping up with prices, housing becomes unattainable, and the general public starts asking why prosperity seems to flow only ever upward, point their anger sideways. Declare yesterday's workers today's invaders. Expand state power in the name of security. Fracture the coalition that might otherwise have demanded structural reform. America has repeated some version of this cycle for more than 150 years. The names change. The targeted communities change. The political slogans change. The underlying mechanism? Barely does. I want to show you the pattern. Because once you see it in the historical record, today's headlines stop looking like isolated events and start looking like another chapter in a very old American story. And because this time, that story reached my own family. Let's look at the structure, the history, the unprecedented advantages our generation has, and the levers for intervention we can pull. | | ---|---|--- Photo by on The First Model We Need to Understand An article is making the rounds on Substack, answering the question most folks don't even want to ask aloud yet: "" It's built on Peter Turchin's analysis of historical patterns of collapsing societies. Turns out, that can be mathematically modeled with strong predictive power: not prophesy, but systemic analysis with enough rigor to identify conditions that immediately precede structural disruption: revolution, civil war, collapse, conquest, reform, etc. Mapping when societies have accumulated socioeconomic conditions equivalent to an oversupply of deadwood in a forest... you can tell that the conditions are ripe for a wildfire, even if you can't exactly predict the spark. His theory -- based on rigorous mathematical analysis of over 5,000 historical examples -- pivots on three major societal characteristics. 1. "Popular Immiseration ": This is what happens when wages and salary detach from growth, as we've all endured in America for the past 50 years; acutely for the past 30. The number of years your parents had to work to buy their first home, versus the number your kids will have to work to achieve the same milestone, is a precisely personal measure of "popular immiseration." The ~25% decline in actual American standard of living since my childhood in the 1990s, is a measure. Our record-levels of indebtedness, the suffocating student loans, the inability to afford healthcare or housing or even a $400 emergency expense for vast numbers of Americans... that's "popular immiseration," and it is the raw fuel for chaos or revolution. 2. The "Wealth Pump ": Economic and political structures that systematically transfer wealth from the middle and lower classes, to the upper echelon. Here we're talking about corporate monopolies, wage extraction, price gouging... every mechanism of billionaire profits at everyone else's expense - and, crucially, the political protection, complicity, endorsement, or outright facilitation of such extraction. This is the engine of both popular immiseration and the creation of an elite crust of society, who are disconnected financially and empathetically from the vast majority of their countryfolk. Think about the attitude of the health insurance and pharma CEOs vs. Americans who actually need healthcare. The billionaires vs. everyone else. As Occupy Wall Street so memorably put it, the 1% vs. the 99%. (Although it's closer to the 0.0001%.) Of note: America is currently suffering from levels of wealth inequality that rival the conditions that gave rise to the French Revolution. Marie Antoinette? Versailles? "Let them eat cake?" Yeah. No surprise to anyone reading this I'm sure, but... we're there. 3. "Elite Overproduction " and competition: Here is where it gets interesting. Revolutions throughout history -- including the American Revolution -- generally have not been led by the peasants or the poor folks themselves. The leaders are -- almost universally -- people who should be of high status in their societies: upper-middle class upbringing, well educated, raised with the presumption that economic and/or political power were reasonable to expect from their future. But when a society has too many of such people, and too few actual positions for them (...how many college graduates does America have? how many of us cannot find work?...), the resulting competition for scarce status leads some -- a critical few, the spark -- to build power outside of the current structures. Historically speaking, disaffected potential elites harness the anger of the many to catalyze rebellion, structural reform, and/or revolutionary change. Now, these three factors have all been at dangerously high levels in American society for some time now -- and worsening. Turchin accurately predicted in Nature , back in 2010, that America would go through structural destabilization of some kind or another in the 2020s. Here we are. Which is why his model's predictions for the range of possible outcomes are keenly relevant to today. Put simply: Outright collapse , including conquest by another nation Lasting dictatorship /authoritarian consolidation Civil war , of one kind or another The good option: Broad-based structural reforms that relieve the economic pain of the majority enough to dissipate the pressure. (see below.) a strong piece; and Peter Turchin's analysis is critically important for understanding America today. It 's also missing a layer -- the one many of us, including me, actually live inside. The Layer That's Missing: Nativism as Release Valve There's another very American cycle that's relevant to today, and it has to do with immigration. When labor is needed, immigrants are welcomed. As soon as they establish communities, put down roots, build businesses, begin to aggregate economic and political power... they are rebranded as invaders and/or threats, turned on, and unceremoniously evicted. (A very similar pattern pertains to Black Americans and other oppressed groups within America, not just newcomers.) Once you add that layer on top of Turchin's patterns, our current situation comes into much clearer focus. Here's what the data shows: when Turchin's three pressures build, the conflict they create is supposed to run vertically -- ordinary people versus the small number of people capturing the gains. The 99% versus the 1%. That is how reform is won, or revolution is fought. But that fight almost never happens properly. Instead, elites protect themselves -- and some aspiring elites cynically assist -- by redirecting the pressure horizontally -- worker against worker, neighbor against neighbor. By turning an immigrant community into the scapegoat for a scarcity that concentrated capital actually created. It follows the same six steps almost every time: 1. Labor is invited. The economy needs workers, so a community from another country is welcomed in -- railroads, agriculture, wartime production, care work, whatever the moment demands. 2. The community establishes itself. Over several generations, the community acquires property, builds businesses, earns credentials, gains social standing, sometimes achieves political power. 3. The elite extraction limit hits. Meanwhile, the wealth pump has been a-pumping. Housing and wages diverge. Popular immiseration hits. Credentialed people can't find the positions they were promised. The state starts to look incompetent. Anyone who has prosperity or stability -- who doesn 't look like "us" -- starts to seem like a rival, or a threat. 4. Scapegoating. Rather than tackle structural reckoning with genuine social solidarity, some political faction weaponizes identity. It's entirely too easy to convince a poor white person to blame a poor Mexican person, rather than to blame the billionaire above them. (Particularly if, as now, that poor white person lives in one of the most propagandized societies on earth, and the elites pour money like gasoline into that fiery propaganda, to protect their own interests.) 5. Oppression/Expulsion. Exceptional state power gets normalized -- on noncitizens first. Authoritarianism is tested wherever it looks safest to do so. Raids, detention, deportation, disappearing due process... everything that protects the elite's power, is deployed. While convincing enough of the majority group that "the government is protecting our interests!" to fracture genuine solidarity -- even though, every time, the eviction of immigrant communities actually hurts everyone economically. 6. Repression AND reform. The authoritarian apparatus perfected on immigrants migrates inward. The same tools get turned on citizens, journalists, dissidents, and anyone who objects. While silencing, neutralizing, or marginalizing the designated enemy, the capital-and-political elites also turn their attention to appeasing the in-group. If enough people are protected, entertained, or buffered from the terrorizing of others -- or perversely gratified by it -- genuine solidarity can be sabotaged before it becomes effective enough to win real structural reform that would benefit everyone (except the elites). With true solidarity neutralized, the elites win cover and retain power: 1. First, the immediate pressure of popular anger and immiseration in the in-group is relieved through turning against scapegoated immigrants, even against their own interests. 2. Then, the elites hand out just enough structural reform to improve material conditions for the in-group who remains, relieving the pressure for awhile... while leaving untouched the underlying structural forces (elite power, extraction...) that produced it. This isn't a one-time story. It's the story, five times over. Five times, the same ending Here's the history lesson. (Skip down if you want the likely trajectories from here, our unprecedented advantages, and what you can do to influence how this goes.) Let's take a look at how the intersection of the immigrant "welcome-then-betray" pattern has played out against Turchin's three structural-compromise indicators, throughout the past 150 years of American history. It's eye-opening: 1. Chinese Exclusion (1882). In the 1850s and '60s, Chinese laborers were welcomed because America needed workers--for mines, agriculture, factories, and especially the railroads that made the fortunes of the emerging Gilded Age. Chinese workers built lives and communities alongside the infrastructure they built for the country. Then the depression of the 1870s hit. Wages fell, jobs became scarce, and the robber-baron economy generated immense fortunes above, and widespread insecurity below. Rather than force railroad magnates, financiers, and industrialists to surrender their growing power, political leaders and labor demagogues recast Chinese workers as "unassimilable" competitors responsible for white hardship. The result was mob violence, massacres, forced expulsions, discriminatory local laws, and finally the first major federal law excluding an entire nationality of laborers. The bargain offered to white workers was racial protection in place of economic power: restrict Chinese competition, preserve certain jobs for the in-group, and promise that exclusion would restore security. But the fortunes accumulated by railroad owners and financiers were not redistributed. Corporate power was not broken. White workers did not gain ownership of the economy they had helped build. Exclusion provided enough psychological status and limited labor-market protection to fracture the coalition that might have confronted the robber barons directly. The deeper reckoning arrived later, through the Populist and Progressive movements: antitrust enforcement, railroad regulation, food and workplace protections, democratic reforms, and the beginnings of organized labor power. Those reforms restrained parts of the Gilded Age order--but they developed inside a political system that had already expelled Chinese workers from the coalition entitled to benefit. 2. The Palmer Raids (1919 -20). After World War One, millions of troops were demobilized into the labor market, wartime inflation devoured wages, and workers launched one of the largest strike waves in American history. The Russian Revolution, several genuine anarchist bombings, and elite fear of organized labor were fused into a single manufactured enemy: immigrant, radical, anarchist, socialist, union organizer, "national-security threat." Under Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer and the young J. Edgar Hoover, federal agents raided homes and meeting halls, arrested thousands, and deported hundreds--often without warrants, reliable evidence, access to counsel, or meaningful due process. Immigrant radicals were the most vulnerable targets, but the broader purpose was to terrorize the labor movement and teach native-born workers that solidarity with "foreign agitators" would place them outside respectable American society. In exchange, the protected in-group was offered normalcy: patriotic belonging, relief from wartime upheaval, rising consumer abundance for those able to access it, and a government explicitly aligned with business. The 1920s weakened unions, concentrated wealth, cut taxes at the top, and elevated the businessman and millionaire as national heroes. Repression had relieved the political pressure without repairing the economic structure. Less than a decade later, in the great crash of 1929, the speculative, debt-driven order built on top of that inequality imploded anyway. 3. Mexican Repatriation (1930s). Mexican workers had been actively recruited for American agriculture, mining, railroads, and industry--particularly when World War One and earlier immigration restrictions produced labor shortages. Then the economy built by the Gilded Age's monopolists and the 1920s financial elite collapsed. The people whose work had been indispensable were suddenly blamed for unemployment, falling wages, and pressure on public relief. Local, state, and federal authorities pressured, deceived, rounded up, and transported hundreds of thousands of people across the border. Many were American citizens, including children born here, because the state was never carefully sorting by citizenship. It was sorting by ancestry, surname, neighborhood, and who looked like the designated enemy. At the same time, the New Deal finally delivered a substantial portion of the structural reform Populists, Progressives, unionists, and socialists had demanded for decades: banking regulation, public employment, Social Security, collective-bargaining rights, infrastructure, and new limits on corporate power. Those reforms were real. They materially improved millions of lives, strengthened organized labor, built a mass middle class, and helped save American democracy. But the political settlement was racially bounded. Agricultural and domestic workers were initially excluded from central protections, preserving the power of Southern landowners and other employers while leaving disproportionately Black and Mexican American workers outside much of the new social contract. Repression removed part of the working class; exclusion kept another part cheap and politically weak; reform gave enough security and bargaining power to the protected in-group to stabilize the country. The wealth pump was significantly constrained--but America avoided having to extend equal economic citizenship to everyone whose labor had built it. 4. The Bracero Program and the 1954 deportation campaign. During World War Two, the federal government again faced a labor shortage and created the Bracero Program, importing Mexican men on temporary contracts to work in agriculture and on the railroads. The program continued until 1964 and brought millions of workers into the United States--but on terms that tied their legal presence and economic survival closely to the employers who hired them. Then, in 1954, the government launched a highly publicized, racially named mass-deportation campaign against other Mexican workers and communities, even while growers continued to demand--and the federal government continued to import--Mexican labor. The contradiction reveals the actual structure. The goal was never simply to remove Mexican workers. American agriculture still depended on them. The goal was to separate labor from belonging: to preserve access to the workforce while stripping that workforce of permanence, security, bargaining power, and the practical ability to say no. Employers received a controlled and replaceable labor supply. Native-born workers were told that the government was protecting their jobs and borders. Mexican American citizens were pressured to distinguish themselves from the newly criminalized "illegal" worker, weakening solidarity inside the community itself. Meanwhile, the protected majority received the broader benefits of the postwar settlement--union wages, subsidized mortgages, public infrastructure, expanding education, and the promise of middle-class security--although many of those benefits were distributed through racially discriminatory institutions. The United States could therefore sustain a generous social contract for much of its in-group while keeping a politically vulnerable population available to exploit while performing essential work beneath it. 5. Japanese incarceration. Japanese immigrants had also been welcomed where their labor was needed, particularly in western agriculture. Over time, Japanese American families built farms, businesses, schools, houses of worship, and civic institutions despite laws barring many first-generation immigrants from naturalization and restricting their ability to own land. After Pearl Harbor, wartime fear, racial hostility, economic envy, and claims of national security merged. More than 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry were forcibly removed from their homes and incarcerated; approximately two-thirds were United States citizens. The government did not conduct individualized investigations to determine who had committed an offense. It designated an entire ancestry as presumptively foreign. Families lost homes, farms, businesses, and years of freedom, while neighboring landowners and commercial competitors sometimes acquired the property and economic space they left behind. The majority population was offered both reassurance and material advantage: the government appeared decisive, the internal "threat" appeared contained, and valuable assets and opportunities were transferred away from the targeted community. At the same time, the wartime state delivered extraordinary benefits and social incorporation to much of the protected population--full employment, unionized industrial wages, military benefits, subsidized education, and eventually government-backed pathways into homeownership. Japanese American soldiers could prove their loyalty through exceptional sacrifice, but their families' citizenship had not protected them at home. Once "foreign" becomes a racial category rather than a legal one, citizenship stops functioning as a shield. Every single time, the scapegoating succeeds politically while failing as a genuine economic remedy. It may produce limited advantages for parts of the in-group: one category of job reserved, a competitor expelled, a government benefit extended, a union contract protected, a mortgage subsidized, a feeling of restored status or safety. Those gains are not always imaginary. That is precisely why the bargain works. But they are carefully bounded. They relieve enough pressure to undermine the broader solidarity that could have won deeper change, while leaving the commanding heights of wealth and political power largely intact. And when structural reform finally comes, it comes divided. Antitrust and workplace reform alongside Chinese exclusion. Postwar prosperity alongside deportation and racialized "guest" labor. The New Deal for those its programs were built to include, with Black, Mexican American, agricultural, and domestic workers excluded from crucial protections. The GI Bill and federally supported homeownership administered through systems that blocked many families of color. Liberal democracy and due process for the presumed American in-group; surveillance, detention, expulsion, or dispossession for the population cast as foreign. This is the pattern the Turchin article doesn't name: America 's historical "exit" has rarely been a clean choice between reform and collapse. More often, it has been reform for some, paired with repression of others --enough material protection for the in-group to stabilize the system, purchased through the exclusion, exploitation, or expulsion of the people whose solidarity might otherwise have made deeper transformation possible. The brilliance--and the horror--of the arrangement is that the in-group does receive something. Not enough to become free of elite domination. Not enough to end the wealth pump permanently. But enough to persuade many people that defending their relative position is safer than joining with the designated "enemy" to demand a fundamentally different order. Where we are right now Let's catch up to the present moment and look at the numbers. As of April 2026, ICE was holding more than 60,000 people -- over 70% percent with no criminal conviction at all, and the vast majority of the rest with misdemeanors. But point-in-time detention numbers are only the snapshot; removals are the throughput, and that tells the real story. ICE reported nearly 320,000 removals in FY2025, and early FY2026 data point toward a pace above 430,000 a year. That's hundreds of thousands of hardworking, contributing community members, gone , plus whoever of their family left to follow them. This is not a system narrowly targeting violent criminals. It's one of the largest coercive administrative systems in the federal government, running full-tilt against a politically vulnerable out-group. Meanwhile, V-Dem recorded a historic 24% single-year collapse in the U.S. Liberal Democracy Index, dropping the country from 20th to 51st in the world. And underneath that increase in authoritarianism sits the wealth pump itself: the top 10% of households own more than two-thirds of household wealth, the top 1% alone owns almost as much as the bottom 90 percent combined, and the median home now costs roughly 5x median household income, up from about 3x a generation ago. That's not a prediction. That's the wealth pump, measured, in real time -- running at the exact moment the "foreigner" sorting mechanism is running too. Stages 4 and 5, with forays into 6, are live right now. Inside corporate America, the extraction is even easier to see. Across the S&P 500, CEOs were paid about 285x their median worker in 2024, versus roughly 21x in 1965. What does a nominal $2 wage increase mean to a normal worker, when the CEO used to be making 30x your pay and is now making 300x? Among the 100 major companies with the lowest median wages, the ratio hit 632 to one -- average CEO pay near $17.2 million against a median worker earning $35,570. At Starbucks, the reported ratio topped 6,600 to 1. It's tempting to say America is now more unequal than France on the eve of its revolution. Truthfully -- the records are incomplete, but the comparison is no longer absurd. We've built, inside a nominal democracy, a level of wealth concentration recognizable as aristocratic. The trajectories, briefly Turchin's pattern gives you a range of outcomes: Most likely (roughly even odds): uneven authoritarian consolidation -- elections continue, but detention, surveillance, and selective enforcement quietly expand for whoever's been designated the internal enemy, while daily life stays normal enough for everyone else that the warnings sound exaggerated. Second most likely: an actual reform exit -- the Progressive Era/New Deal kind -- but only if the coalition that wins it refuses to leave anyone out this time. Less likely but not remote: acute civil rupture -- not armies on a front line, necessarily, but other forms of civil war: disputed elections, federal-state standoffs, and political violence that rival elites may start but can't always control. The patterns of American history give you a strong likelihood: Immigrants or racially-profiled minorities will be scapegoated, imprisoned, and expelled. So will anyone who supports them. Authoritarianism may consolidate, and billionaire power will almost certainly persist, but the in-group will be granted enough psychological status and material relief to get them to go along. But. This outcome is not certain. And the direction, magnitude, and impact on individuals will vary widely with local conditions, cross-group solidarity, regional and economic differences, public awareness of these dynamics, and coordinated pushback. There is abundant room to make a difference. Why this time could - truly - be different History repeats itself--but never under identical conditions. There are reasons for hope that previous generations simply did not have. For most of American history, the people being scapegoated were largely unable to tell their own stories. Chinese railroad workers could not livestream an expulsion. Japanese American families could not upload footage from incarceration camps. Mexican American citizens rounded up during the Depression could not instantly show the country what was happening to them. News flowed downward through a handful of newspapers, radio stations, and television networks. If powerful institutions decided on the narrative, most people never encountered an alternative. That world is gone. Today, millions of ordinary people carry cameras in our pockets. A raid in Tacoma can be seen in Miami an hour later. An ICE detention center in Washington can become the concern of a church in Georgia, a veterans' organization in Texas, or a labor union in Michigan. Propaganda still exists--at industrial scale--but so does the ability to document reality before someone else has the chance to rewrite it. Something else is different. America is no longer isolated from the rest of the world. Most of us now have genuine friendships, family ties, professional relationships, and communities that cross national, racial, and religious lines. Millions of Americans have immigrant spouses. Children who speak more than one language. Coworkers from every continent. Veterans who fought beside interpreters they still consider family. Faith communities that are themselves multinational. It is much harder to convince people that "those people" are aliens when "those people" are your neighbors, your coworkers, your son-in-law, your mosque, your church, your child's teacher. The elite playbook still functions. But it doesn't work as automatically as it once did. Most importantly, we understand the pattern better than previous generations did. Peter Turchin's work gives us one lens. History gives us another. We can watch the pressure building. We can recognize the wealth pump. We can see the scapegoating while it is happening--not decades later in a history book. That creates a possibility our predecessors could never reach. The greatest advantage any manipulation has is that the target doesn't realize they're being manipulated. Once enough people recognize the mechanism, it begins to lose its power. The ending is not written. The same American history that teaches us how democracies drift toward oligarchy and turn against the people who built them, also teaches us that ordinary people like you and me, acting together across the lines they were told to fear, have repeatedly forced this country to become more than its elites intended. That possibility still exists. But only if we refuse, this time, to let them convince us that our neighbors are the enemy when the real question has always been who benefits from us fighting each other. What you can actually do Not just "be kinder" -- although building relationships with people you disagree with politically is worthwhile, albeit uncomfortable, and can be a real firebreak , when the spark comes. Here are structural approaches as well: Build solidarity before the emergency , not after -- unions, congregations, neighborhood networks, immigrant-veteran alliances. People defend who they understand as genuinely part of their own "we." Build the "we." Defend due process and the rule of law universally. The moment you accept a lower standard for someone unpopular, you've built the tool that will get used on your friends, your loved ones, and eventually you next. Document everything, rigorously -- names, badge numbers, dates, outcomes. Organize everything. Preserve multiple copies. Save it offline, in local storage and physical locations. Share it with trusted friends. Evidentiary architecture is what lets the truth survive contact with power. Ask me how I know. Make healthcare and housing a democracyissue -- because a generation that can't form a household, access medical care, or believe in the future is a generation susceptible to manipulation, gaslighting, and temptation to join the enforcers (eg. ICE) out of sheer economic desperation. Create honorable off-ramps for elite defectors -- When people who hold power -- of any kind, financial, civil, political, social... -- decide that they don't want to uphold this regime anymore, welcome them. They are essential for actual victory. Demanding humiliation from new allies is a strong disincentive for them to come join us...and we need them. Reform happens when elite defection is possible and rewarded, not just when protest is loud. Share the knowledge. The more people can see through the pattern, the better chance we all have of successfully resisting the gaslighting, scapegoating, bribery, betrayal, and propaganda machine being used on us in real-time. We can break this pattern... but we have to do it together. This is personal My husband, Zahid, is an honorable, patriotic, decorated, 100% disabled United States military veteran. He has lived in America for decades. He is disabled in wheelchair due to injuries sustained on active duty. He survived a broken back and traumatic brain injury, among other injuries, in service to this country. He has no U.S. criminal record. He is the father of our two young American children. Last year, ICE illegally abducted him and locked him inside the Northwest ICE Processing Center for 124 days anyway. That happened because the sorting mechanism I have described throughout this article is real. Once institutions begin sorting people primarily into categories instead of judging them as individuals under the law, the facts that ought to matter begin to disappear. Military service. Disability. Family. Character. Decades of contributing to our community. None of it protected him. The machinery had decided which box he belonged in. So we fought. Not just in the court of public opinion. In federal court. In immigration court. At the BIA. In the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, one level below the Supreme Court. Across four separate federal jurisdictions, with no attorney. We documented everything. We challenged everything. We refused to disappear quietly into the administrative machinery of state terror. And eventually, a federal judge ordered Zahid's immediate release, concluding that what had happened was, in the court's own words, "flat out wrong." (Chaudhry v. Bondi , No. 2:25-cv-02339, W.D. Wash.) I'm not telling you this because it's extraordinary. I 'm telling you because it isn't. It is exactly what this historical pattern predicts: extraordinary coercive power first deployed against the people least likely to be defended, justified by broad categories instead of individualized justice, and normalized one case at a time. The only reason you know Zahid's name, instead of one of the hundreds of thousands of others who pass through that system, is that we refused to let his story disappear. If you want someone in Congress who has not only studied these patterns in history, but has stood inside them--who has defended constitutional due process when it landed like a meteor in my life, who has confronted a weaponized federal government and prevailed, who knows from lived experience what abusive government power feels like when it is turned against an ordinary family--I'm asking for your vote, your voice, and whatever support you can give. I'm Melissa Chaudhry: a Constitutional Democrat, community-rooted leader, published author, and proven fighter for liberty and justice. I don't answer to corporate PACs, foreign interests, or defense contractors. I answer to the Constitution of the United States of America -- and to We the People, who only get real victory if we fighttogether. # Just The Truth
Your No-BS NewsletterDear Readers,Today's sponsor, the International Mission Board (IMB), is highlighting a unique opportunity that will accompany one of the world's largest sporting events. As millions of visitors travel to North America for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, IMB is preparing to equip volunteers with Scripture, outreach materials, and discipleship resources to share the Gospel with people from around the world—many of whom may have little or no opportunity to hear the Christian message in their home countries. Read the message below to learn more about IMB's World Cup outreach efforts and how you can support the mission.Thank you for your consideration of our sponsors.
The Just The Truth Team
